planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into moist, fertile soil; give this selection room to form a full clump since it will not reach peak bloom density until its second year.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; 'Firetail' is the most widely planted mountain fleece selection, an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner prized for slender, upright, bottle-brush spikes of intense crimson-red held well above the heart-shaped leaf mound from midsummer clear through the first hard frost. The plump, non-spreading clump forms a dense weed-suppressing mass that needs no staking even at full size. Deadheading spent spikes tidies the display but is not required for continued bloom, since new spikes are produced continuously along the season. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to renew vigor.

common_name: Taurus Red Bistort (Compact Extended-Bloom Mountain Fleece)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into moist, moderately fertile soil; 'Taurus' forms a bushy, self-supporting clump and needs no staking even in the widest part of its spread.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, moderately fertile soil; 'Taurus' is a sturdy, shorter-statured mountain fleece selection that produces its deep crimson-red bottlebrush spikes over an especially long window, from midsummer into late fall, on a bushy clump that resists flopping better than the straight species. Its more compact height makes it easier to place near the front or middle of a moisture-retentive border than taller mountain fleece cultivars. Bumblebees and other pollinators visit the spikes steadily through the bloom season. Divide crowded clumps in early spring every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring into moist, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed; this sterile, clump-forming selection does not spread by stolons the way the species can, so it stays where it is planted.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in evenly moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil; 'Red Dragon' is grown chiefly for its foliage, which opens purple-red with a smoky gray-green chevron marking, ages to a silvery purple-and-green wash, and finally settles to green with maturity, giving the plant three distinct looks across a single season. Wiry red stems carry small white to pale pink flower spikes in late summer, but the leaf color is the main draw and pairs well against dark-leaved neighbors in a shaded border. As a sterile, clump-forming cultivar it will not self-sow or run the way seed-grown Persicaria species can, making it a tidier choice for mixed plantings. In zones below its hardiness range it can be grown as a striking annual foliage accent.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Geisha' spreads by rhizomes far more slowly than the straight species, but still benefits from a check every few years if grown among smaller companions.

directions: Grow in partial shade to mostly shaded sites in moist, humus-rich soil; 'Geisha' is a variegated sport of gooseneck loosestrife whose mint-green leaves carry an irregular, jagged cream-white margin, turning soft coral-pink tones in fall for a second season of interest that the plain species lacks. Arching, swan-necked spikes of small white flowers appear in mid- to late summer and make a distinctive, long-lasting cut flower. Selected specifically for a much less aggressive spreading habit than the straight species, it is far better suited to mixed shade borders where gooseneck loosestrife's usual thuggish colonizing would be unwelcome. Consistent moisture keeps the variegated leaf margins from scorching in brighter sites.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Firecracker' spreads by rhizomes like the species and is best sited where a colonizing native perennial is welcome or where it can be contained.

directions: Grow in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Firecracker' is a dark-leaved selection of the North American native fringed loosestrife, its pointed foliage emerging deep burgundy in spring and holding rich purple-bronze margins through summer, a striking foil for the small, star-shaped, bright yellow flowers produced along arching stems in early to midsummer. Like the species it spreads steadily by rhizomes in moist, fertile ground, forming an expanding colony rather than a tidy clump, so give it room or a root barrier in smaller borders. It remains an excellent native nectar source for small bees, including pollen specialists of the genus Macropis, while adding dark foliage color the plain green species lacks. Divide congested colonies in spring to share and to keep the foliage color fresh.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Alexander' spreads by rhizomes but at a noticeably slower rate than the straight species and rarely sets viable seed.

directions: Grow in partial shade to full sun in moist to moderately dry, fertile soil; 'Alexander' is a variegated sport of yellow loosestrife, its whorled, serrated leaves edged in creamy white that emerges with a pink blush in spring before settling to a crisp cream margin for the rest of the season. Cup-shaped, golden-yellow flowers with a red-tinged throat appear in loose spikes through early and midsummer, but the season-long variegated foliage is the main ornamental feature. It spreads by rhizomes less aggressively than the plain species and rarely produces viable seed, making it a better-mannered choice for a partly shaded border. Keep soil from drying out completely, since the variegated leaf margins brown quickly under drought stress.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist to wet, fertile soil; this compact selection is well suited to containers as well as garden beds, unlike larger turtlehead cultivars.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil; 'Tiny Tortuga' is a compact descendant of the popular 'Hot Lips' turtlehead, bred down to roughly half the height of typical Chelone obliqua selections while keeping the same glossy, dark bronze-green foliage and hooded, hot-pink, snapdragon-like flower spikes from mid- to late summer into fall. Its small stature and slowly spreading rhizomes make it a good fit for rain gardens, pond edges, and containers where full-size turtleheads would quickly outgrow the space. Bumblebees, among the few insects strong enough to force open the pinched flower mouth, are its main pollinators. It tolerates heavier soils and somewhat wider temperature swings than older turtlehead cultivars, but still performs best where soil moisture never runs short.

common_name: Summer Snow Obedient Plant (White False Dragonhead)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring or early fall into moist, fertile soil; 'Summer Snow' spreads by rhizomes like most obedient plant cultivars, so divide every two to three years to keep it within bounds.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; 'Summer Snow' is a pure white-flowered cultivar of obedient plant, producing dense, upright spikes of tubular, two-lipped blooms on stiff, square stems from midsummer through early fall, earlier and often longer than many pink cultivars. Like other Physostegia, individual florets stay put when nudged to a new position on the spike, the quirk that gives the genus its common name. The bright white spikes read especially well against dark-foliaged neighbors in a partly shaded border and make a long-lasting cut flower. It spreads by rhizomes at a similar pace to other straight-species-derived cultivars, so plan to divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain a tidy footprint and strong flowering.
